lines: If the city power cuts out completely, do not light a single candle inside your room.
Candles cause dangerous house fires during blackouts, and Jack knows the grid will stay dead for days.
Suddenly, every skyscraper window goes completely pitch black across the entire downtown skyline at 10 PM.
Jack immediately moves away from the pitch black streets and walks toward his tall office building shelter.
Panicked drivers honk on gridlocked roads, but Jack keeps moving fast toward safety.
He reaches the heavy lobby doors and steps safely inside the fortified building.
One. Store water early by filling every container and bathtub while the water taps still work.
Gravity tanks empty fast during a blackout, so Jack secures clean emergency drinking water immediately.
Two. Use battery flashlights for illumination instead of matches because open flames trigger deadly building fires.
Jack clicks on his durable LED flashlight, lighting the dark interior without risking any fire danger.
Three. Keep the fridge and freezer shut tight to preserve every ounce of your perishable food.
A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours, and a full freezer lasts 48 hours.
Jack also knows to never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors because carbon monoxide kills silently.
He has clean water, safe battery light, and cold rations secured inside his locked high-rise office.
It was the perfect blackout survival plan, but there was just one terrible problem.
Heavy smoke begins pouring from under the stairwell door, and all exit alarms are dead.
part1.cliffhanger: Toxic smoke fills the stairwell while the building alarms are completely dead, trapping Jack high up in the dark.

lines: Part two. Toxic smoke fills the high stairwell while all emergency alarms remain totally dead.
Someone downstairs lit emergency candles, sparking an uncontrolled fire across the lower office floors.
All streetlights and grid power stay dead, leaving the entire city in freezing blackness.
Jack quickly retreats backward and walks toward his backup office shelter on the safe side.
Scared workers cough down the hall, but Jack urges everyone to stay low and calm.
He pulls his team inside the secondary suite and shuts the heavy fire door securely.
One. Never open doors that feel warm, and seal all door cracks with wet clothing.
Jack uses his stored water to soak jackets, blocking deadly carbon monoxide from seeping inside.
Two. Never run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors because carbon monoxide kills silently.
Panicked survivors downstairs try starting a gas stove, but Jack warns them through the doorway.
Three. Conserve battery flashlights and avoid breathing toxic smoke by staying low against the floor.
Jack clicks his LED flashlight to low power, preserving critical visibility through the pitch dark.
Remember that a closed fridge keeps food safe 4 hours and full freezers 48 hours.
Jack shares emergency cold rations and clean bottled water with the stranded workers beside him.
Sirens finally echo outside as city firefighters battle the blaze and clear the lower floors.
Fire crews reach Jack's sealed safe room and guide everyone down through the safe stairwell.
Use flashlights instead of candles during blackouts. Follow for a new scenario tomorrow.
draft_morning.title: Trapped in a Blackout Fire: Survival Part 2
draft_morning.description: Jack faces toxic smoke in a city-wide blackout after an office building catches fire. Here is the safest way to survive trapped in a dark skyscraper.
